analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from using pricing algorithms that inflate rents, and lets renters sue.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in January 2024 and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for landlords of four or more rental units to use pricing software that pools rent and supply data from many landlords and recommends prices. Using such a service would count automatically as an illegal price-fixing scheme under the antitrust laws, and the FTC, the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and renters themselves could all sue. It would also void forced-arbitration clauses so renters could take these companies to court. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters, who would be protected from rent-setting algorithms that pool competitor data across many landlords and push rents upward; the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general would gain new enforcement tools.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a per se Sherman Act violation for a rental property owner with 4 or more units to pay for a pricing coordinator's services, meaning a court would not need to weigh justifications before finding it illegal [S2].

It defines the banned 'coordinating function' as collecting prices, supply, and lease-renewal data from multiple landlords, processing it computationally, and recommending rents, renewal terms, or occupancy levels [S2].
It gives enforcement power to the FTC, the Attorney General, and state attorneys general, and lets any aggrieved renter sue for triple damages plus attorney fees [S2].
A renter can elect to have pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers voided for claims under the Act, keeping the case in court [S2].
It lowers pleading standards for these cases: a complaint citing consciously parallel pricing coordination counts as plausible, without needing to rule out independent pricing [S2].
It also blocks one pricing-software company from acquiring another if the deal would lessen competition, and does not preempt stronger state or local laws [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Rental property owners with 4 or more units, and the pricing-software companies (such as revenue-management services used by large landlords) that would lose that business or face antitrust liability; mergers among such firms could be blocked.

drawbacks.text: The bill's per se ban and relaxed pleading standard sweep broadly: any software that pools data from multiple landlords and recommends prices would be illegal, which could also capture legitimate pricing tools that help small landlords price fairly, and critics would argue it deters lawful competition on services rather than just collusion.

Landlords could argue rents reflect many factors (supply, demand, local regulations) and that a blanket per se rule, rather than a case-by-case antitrust inquiry, is an overly rigid way to police a new technology.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to renters could be substantial if algorithmic rent-setting is raising rents across markets, and the bill preserves court access and state-level enforcement. The cost is that a per se rule is a blunt instrument: it bans entire categories of data-pooling software rather than policing specific schemes, which risks sweeping in tools that some landlords use innocently. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much these algorithms actually raise rents, which the bill assumes rather than measures.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on January 30, 2024, with seven original Democratic cosponsors [S2].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, its only action [S1].
It gathered 10 cosponsors (9 Democrats and 1 Independent), all Democrats or allied independents, but no Republican [S3].
The Judiciary Committee never held a hearing or markup, no further action appears in the record, and the bill expired with the 118th Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large landlords and pricing-software companies are better off: no court or agency can act on the conduct the bill targeted, and the status quo of algorithmic rent-setting continues. Renters gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 9 Democratic and 1 Independent cosponsor, but had no committee chair's support to move it.

for.name: Sens. Welch, Klobuchar, Sanders, Blumenthal, Hirono, Butler, and Merkley
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill; Klobuchar chairs the Senate antitrust subcommittee but the bill still never got committee action.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the 15 months it had jurisdiction, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Revenue-management software providers and large landlords
against.role: Industry whose product and practices the bill would outlaw
against.what_they_did: No lobbying appears in the record, but as the regulated parties they had a strong stake in the bill not advancing; related lawsuits over rent-setting algorithms were pending against major providers and landlords during this period.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican supported it, and the Democratic-run Judiciary Committee also never advanced it.

industries.note: These firms pool rent and supply data from many landlords and recommend prices; the bill would make their core service illegal for large landlords and expose mergers among them to antitrust blocks. Renters bear the cost of these algorithms through higher rents, so the firms' interest runs against theirs.

They would be barred from using such pricing services, face per se antitrust liability, and be open to triple-damage suits by renters whose forced-arbitration clauses would be void. Their savings from coordinated pricing come out of renters' pockets.
The bill gives them explicit new authority over this conduct, including independent FTC litigation power and easier pleading standards.
